name: Canthaxanthin
lead: Canthaxanthin is an orange-red keto-carotenoid pigment (C40H52O2) found in some mushrooms, algae, bacteria and crustaceans, and used as a food and feed colourant, for example to colour farmed salmon, trout and egg yolks [1][2][3]. When swallowed in large amounts, it deposits in fat beneath the skin and gives a golden-orange tint, which is why it was sold in oral 'tanning pills' [1].

This colour is not melanin-based. High-dose tanning-pill use has been associated with canthaxanthin retinopathy, in which yellow crystalline deposits appear in the retina, and with reports of urticaria and liver injury, according to the US FDA and the American Academy of Dermatology as summarised on Wikipedia [1][4]. The FDA has no tanning pills approved for sale in the US and has sent warning letters to firms marketing canthaxanthin pills as 'adulterated cosmetics' with an unsafe colour additive [1].

Controlled human studies from the 1970s and 1980s combined canthaxanthin with beta-carotene in photodermatoses and as an oral skin-colouring agent [5][6][7]. It is discussed on T Nation and other forums from the early 2000s as a possible pill for a tan-like colour [14][16][17].

Feed/food colourant; formerly oral tanning pills [1]

paras: Taken orally at high doses, canthaxanthin imparts a golden-orange hue to skin through deposition in subcutaneous fat [1]. A forum poster in 2001 described it as available at health food stores as a food-colour additive that was 'not exactly legal for tanning purposes' [14], and another described an orange tone appearing before a tan-like look [17][15].

It has been given with beta-carotene to patients with photodermatoses and pigmentation disorders [5][6], tested alongside beta-carotene in photochemotherapy for psoriasis [7], and the combined preparation's plasma levels were studied during and after stopping intake [8]. As a food colourant, it is approved in the US and EU but not in Australia and New Zealand, with EU feed limits of 80 mg/kg of feedstuffs (lower for laying hens and poultry) [1].

A 1985 clinical trial examined photoprotection and skin colouring by oral carotenoids [5]. A combined preparation of beta-carotene (25 mg) and canthaxanthin (35 mg) was investigated in 74 patients with photodermatoses and 111 with pigmentation disorders, with ophthalmological controls in 23 patients reporting no abnormalities in that report [9]. A 1978 study examined canthaxanthin in porphyria skin manifestations [6], and a 1984 randomized comparative trial examined beta-carotene/canthaxanthin with photochemotherapy in psoriasis [7].

On the safety side, a registered long-term observation of canthaxanthin retinopathy began in 1983 with 35 participants [12]. Multimodal imaging studies have mapped the extent of retinal involvement in crystalline retinopathy [11], and clinical reviews list canthaxanthin among causes of drug-induced flecked-retina disorders [4]. No modern randomized trial has tested canthaxanthin as a cosmetic tanning pill.

Canthaxanthin retinopathy is a reversible deposition of crystals in the retina reported in a limited number of people who consumed very high amounts via tanning pills; Wikipedia states deposits disappeared after the pills were stopped, while the reviewed literature on flecked retinas lists it as an iatrogenic cause [1][4]. Other reported problems include liver injury and urticaria [1]. A 1991 commentary discussed canthaxanthin toxicity [10], and a Grokipedia summary also mentions rare aplastic anaemia reports [2].
Wikipedia notes that intake from poultry products is far below tanning-pill doses; Wikipedia says reaching similar intake would require more than 50 eggs per day from hens fed practical levels [1].

Canthaxanthin is a fat-soluble antioxidant carotenoid whose biological functions are related at least partly to free-radical scavenging [1][3]. It is biosynthesised from beta-carotene by a ketolase enzyme that adds carbonyl groups at carbons 4 and 4' [1]. In humans its enrichment of LDL has been studied for protection from oxidation, with many health-benefit studies being in vitro [3].

Canthaxanthin was first isolated from edible mushrooms [1]. In the late 1980s, its safety as a food and feed additive was questioned after retinal crystal deposits were found in people who took very high amounts via tanning pills, prompting regulatory review [1].
It is a permitted food colour (E161g) in several jurisdictions but is not approved for tanning use; the FDA treats tanning pills containing it as adulterated cosmetics [1].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and fitness communities
paras: T Nation threads from 2001 to 2003 ask about taking canthaxanthin as a tan, with some users describing it as natural and others asking for experiences and side effects [16][18][17][15]. A 2003 diet thread notes that farmed salmon is coloured with it [13].

timeline.event: Retinal crystal deposits reported in users of high-dose tanning pills. [1]
Long-term observational study of canthaxanthin retinopathy begins. [12]

lore.intro: On T Nation in the early 2000s, canthaxanthin is raised as a pill-based route to a tan-like colour, usually with requests for firsthand experience [16][18][17].

claims.believers: Posters describe it as an oral product that makes you look more tan, though one notes an orange colour appears first [17][15].
claims.experts: It deposits in subcutaneous fat, giving a golden-orange hue rather than melanin pigmentation [1].

claims.claim: It is natural and therefore safe
claims.believers: One poster called it 100 percent natural like beta-carotene [15].
claims.experts: High-dose use has been associated with retinal crystal deposits, urticaria and liver injury; FDA has warned against it [1][4].

claims.claim: It is legal over the counter
claims.believers: A poster says it is available at health food stores but not exactly legal for tanning [14].
claims.experts: The FDA has approved no tanning pills and has sent warning letters [1].

claims.claim: The same pigment colours farmed salmon
claims.believers: A poster notes farm-raised salmon is fed it to colour the flesh [13].
claims.experts: It is used in feed for salmonids and poultry within EU limits [1].
